title: AutoMetrics: Build a Scoring System from Scraps
one_liner: Instead of hiring humans to score every output, AutoMetrics learns to blend simple metrics and AI judges so a few hundred human ratings can guide millions.
lead: Every AI chatbot or travel planner needs a way to know when it is working well. Humans score outputs by hand, but that is expensive and slow. AutoMetrics solves this by learning to mix simple scoring rules and LLM-as-a-Judge into a single automatic scorer that matches human judgment — and it does this with fewer than 100 human labels.

problem.h2: Human judgment is the only true measure, but it is too slow
paras: When you build a chatbot or a travel planner, you need to know: is the output good or bad? A human can tell by reading and rating each answer. But humans are slow and expensive. You need hundreds or thousands of ratings to train a system. If you want to improve the system and test your changes, you need even more human ratings, because every tweak requires validation — your budget for human judgment runs dry quickly.

A naive attempt is to use one fixed automatic scorer — count the right keywords, measure how long the answer is, or ask an LLM to rate it. But a fixed scorer does not know what humans actually value. It might reward long answers when humans want short ones. It might count keywords that do not matter.

callout.html: Humans are the ground truth, but they are expensive. Fixed automatic scorers are fast but wrong. AutoMetrics learns to blend simple metrics and LLM judges so that a small human signal (fewer than 100 ratings) can guide millions of automatic scores.

steps.text: A shelf of 48 pre-built metrics (keywords, length, syntax checks, LLM ratings).
Prompt an LLM: For this task, what makes a good answer? Get domain-specific criteria.
Have humans rate a few hundred outputs (thumbs up/down, or a score).
Regression: which metrics + judges predict human ratings? Weight each one.
Use the learned blend to score new outputs automatically, instantly.

paras: AutoMetrics changes how an automatic scorer is built. Normally, you either hand-craft a single formula (e.g., count specific words) or you use a black-box LLM judge. AutoMetrics instead creates a learned formula that mixes both kinds of signals — simple metrics and LLM judgment — so the mixture is tailored to what your humans actually care about.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: How well does the automatic scorer match human judgment?
hidden.name: correlation with human ratings
paras: The paper measures one central quantity: the correlation, a number from 0 to 1 that says how closely the automatic scorer's outputs match human ratings. If humans rate an output as excellent and the automatic scorer also scores it high, the correlation is high. If they disagree often, the correlation is low.

AutoMetrics estimates this correlation from a small set of human ratings (fewer than 100). It then tunes the blend of metrics and judges to maximize this correlation, so the final formula becomes a faithful proxy for human judgment.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger weight in the learned blend. Highlights show which metrics/judges the paper trusted.

reads.html: Correlation tells you: of 100 outputs a human rated, how many did the automatic scorer rank in the same order? High correlation means the automatic scorer is a trustworthy stand-in.

AutoMetrics optimizes Kendall correlation (a rank-based measure) between the automatic scorer and human ratings. It searches over metric subsets and judge prompts to find the combination that maximizes this correlation on held-out data.

mechanism.h2: Why mixing simple metrics with LLM judges works
paras: No single scorer is universally true. A keyword counter works for some tasks (e.g., extractive summarization) but misses nuance in others (e.g., creative writing). An LLM judge is flexible but expensive and can hallucinate. Combining them lets you cover more ground.

A small human signal (fewer than 100 ratings) acts as a compass. It shows which of your candidate scorers (metrics and LLM judges) actually track human judgment. Regression is the glue: it learns a weight for each candidate scorer, so the weighted average becomes a faithful proxy. The human labels are scarce but trustworthy; the candidate scorers are abundant but noisy. Regression finds the mix that lets the noisy scorers track the truth.

This works because the candidate scorers are diverse. A metric might catch one aspect of quality (e.g., length); an LLM judge might catch another (e.g., coherence). In combination, they cover more of what humans care about.

stages.s: Run all 48 base metrics (keyword counts, length, syntax, etc.)
Ask LLM: generate task-specific judgment criteria
Blend all scores via learned regression weights

math.words: final_score = weight_1 * metric_1 + weight_2 * metric_2 + ... + weight_N * metric_N
symbols: the final automatic rating of the output, 0 to 1
the learned weight for metric or judge criterion i
the score (0 to 1) of the output from metric or criterion i

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose you have 4 scorers: keyword-match, answer-length, LLM-judge-1, LLM-judge-2.
Regression on 100 human ratings learns: w1=0.3, w2=0.1, w3=0.4, w4=0.2.
A new output scores: keyword=0.6, length=0.7, LLM-1=0.8, LLM-2=0.5.
The LLM judges (weights 0.4 and 0.2) dominate the blend, so they drive the final score.

math.note: Regression finds the weights that make the weighted blend match human ratings as closely as possible.

bars.h2: How much does AutoMetrics improve over the baseline?

charts.title: One fixed LLM judge
charts.note: A single LLM judge gives some signal but does not adapt to the task.

charts.title: AutoMetrics
charts.note: By blending task-specific metrics and LLM judges learned from tiny human signal, correlation jumps 20+ points.

items.html: If the 100 human raters all prefer long answers, the regression will weight any metric that correlates with length, even if real human diversity wants short answers. Fix: use diverse human raters, or sample from real usage.
An LLM prompted to judge might invent criteria that sound good but do not match human values. Fix: validate LLM-generated criteria against human feedback; filter out criteria that diverge.

If two metrics measure nearly the same thing (e.g., two length-based metrics), regression will arbitrarily split the weight between them instead of combining their signal cleanly. Fix: pre-filter metrics for diversity, or gently steer weights away from overtuning to noise (e.g., add a penalty for extreme weights).

Use enough diversity in human raters, test LLM-generated criteria against real human ratings to make sure they align, and choose a diverse set of candidate metrics. With 100+ human labels and diverse signals, AutoMetrics becomes a trustworthy automatic scorer.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny demo: pick one open-ended task (e.g., generate a travel recommendation, summarize a news article, answer a trivia question). Collect outputs from your system (or off-the-shelf). Have 50 humans rate each output on a 1-5 scale. Curate 5 simple metrics (e.g., answer length, keyword overlap with a reference, LLM yes/no judgment on a criterion). Generate 3 more LLM judgment criteria. Use AutoMetrics to learn the blend from 40 human ratings, and measure correlation on the held-out 10 ratings. Then compare how much the learned blend outperforms any single metric or LLM judge — the blend should rank outputs more similarly to humans because it can weight whichever signals actually matter for that task.
demo.closing: The demo makes it clear: one fixed scorer is predictable and brittle because it applies the same formula to every task; a learned blend is adaptive because it re-weights the signals for each new domain, so it stays faithful to human judgment wherever it changes.
